--- title: "Flow fields from scratch in Python" subtitle: "Particles drifting through a grid of angles: the gateway drug of generative art." description: "How flow fields work, built up step by step in NumPy and matplotlib: the field, one particle, thousands of particles, smoother noise and a few variations." date: 2026-10-05 categories: [Art, Python, generative] image: ../../../assets/svg/illustrations/palette.svg jupyter: python3 --- If you've seen generative art that looks like hair, smoke, wind or wood grain, there's a good chance it was a **flow field**. The idea is tiny: cover the canvas with arrows, drop some particles on it, and let each particle follow the arrow underneath it. The arrows decide the shape, the particles reveal it. This post builds one from scratch in NumPy and matplotlib. No creative-coding framework, nothing to install beyond what you already have for data work. ## The recipe ```{mermaid} flowchart LR A[Define an angle
for every point] --> B[Scatter particles] B --> C[Look up the angle
under each particle] C --> D[Step a little way
in that direction] D --> C D --> E[Draw the paths] ``` ## 1. The field A flow field is a function that takes a position `(x, y)` and returns an **angle**. Any function will do. Here's one made from a couple of sine waves: ::: {#e977e38e .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} def angle(x, y): return 3.2 * np.sin(2.4 * x) * np.cos(3.1 * y) + 1.4 * np.sin(5 * y) ``` ::: Drawing the angle as an arrow at each point of a coarse grid shows the "wind" the particles will feel: ::: {#cell-fig-field .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} xs, ys = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(0, 1, 40), np.linspace(0, 0.62, 25)) a = angle(xs, ys) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5.6), facecolor="white") ax.quiver(xs, ys, np.cos(a), np.sin(a), a, cmap="viridis", pivot="mid", scale=55, width=0.0025, headwidth=3.5) ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_axis_off() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The angle function drawn as arrows on a 40 × 25 grid.](index_files/figure-html/fig-field-output-1.png){#fig-field width=787 height=496} ::: ::: You can already see the structure: swirls, ridges and calm channels. Everything that follows is just a nicer way of looking at this picture. ## 2. One particle A particle starts somewhere, reads the angle under it, takes a small step in that direction and repeats. That's [Euler integration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler_method), the simplest possible way to follow a field. ::: {#fda9472b .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} def trace(x, y, steps=200, step_size=0.004): path = [(x, y)] for _ in range(steps): a = angle(x, y) x, y = x + step_size * np.cos(a), y + step_size * np.sin(a) path.append((x, y)) return np.array(path) ``` ::: ::: {#cell-fig-one .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5.6), facecolor="white") ax.quiver(xs, ys, np.cos(a), np.sin(a), color="#d8e4cb", pivot="mid", scale=55, width=0.0025, headwidth=3.5) for (x0, y0), c in zip([(.1, .1), (.3, .5), (.55, .2), (.75, .45), (.9, .1)], ["#197050", "#2f9b99", "#c96384", "#e0a526", "#3ab533"]): p = trace(x0, y0) ax.plot(p[:, 0], p[:, 1], lw=3, color=c, solid_capstyle="round") ax.plot(x0, y0, "o", ms=9, color=c, mec=FOREST, mew=1.5) ax.set_xlim(0, 1); ax.set_ylim(0, .62); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_axis_off() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Five particles following the field. Each dot is a starting point.](index_files/figure-html/fig-one-output-1.png){#fig-one width=787 height=496} ::: ::: ## 3. Thousands of particles Tracing particles one at a time in a Python loop gets slow. NumPy lets us move **all** of them at once: keep their positions in two arrays and update every particle in each step. `LineCollection` then draws thousands of paths in one go. ::: {#dbec8b44 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} def flow(angle_fn, n=2000, steps=140, step_size=0.0035, seed=7, w=1.0, h=0.62, starts=None): """Return an (n, steps+1, 2) array of particle paths.""" rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) if starts is None: x, y = rng.uniform(0, w, n), rng.uniform(0, h, n) else: x, y = starts paths = np.empty((len(x), steps + 1, 2)) paths[:, 0] = np.column_stack([x, y]) for i in range(1, steps + 1): a = angle_fn(x, y) x, y = x + step_size * np.cos(a), y + step_size * np.sin(a) paths[:, i] = np.column_stack([x, y]) return paths def draw(paths, colours, bg=FOREST, lw=0.7, alpha=0.6, size=(10, 6.2), ax=None, w=1.0, h=0.62): if ax is None: fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=size, facecolor=bg) ax.set_facecolor(bg) cols = [colours[i % len(colours)] for i in range(len(paths))] ax.add_collection(LineCollection(paths, colors=cols, linewidths=lw, alpha=alpha, capstyle="round")) ax.set_xlim(0, w); ax.set_ylim(0, h); ax.set_aspect("equal") ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]) # hide axes but keep the background for spine in ax.spines.values(): spine.set_visible(False) return ax ``` ::: ::: {#cell-fig-flow .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} draw(flow(angle), DUSK) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![2,000 particles, 140 steps each.](index_files/figure-html/fig-flow-output-1.png){#fig-flow width=869 height=547} ::: ::: That's the core technique. The rest of this post is about changing one ingredient at a time. ## 4. Smoother fields with noise Sine waves repeat, and you can feel the repetition. Most flow-field art uses **noise** instead: smooth randomness that wanders without repeating. Perlin noise is the classic choice, but a simple "value noise" does the job in a few lines. It works like this: put random numbers on a coarse grid, blend smoothly between them, then add a few finer layers on top. ::: {#064f28d1 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} def value_noise(seed=1, res=6, octaves=3): rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) grids = [rng.random((res * 2**o + 2, res * 2**o + 2)) for o in range(octaves)] def sample(x, y): total, amp, norm = 0.0, 1.0, 0.0 for o, g in enumerate(grids): r = res * 2**o gx, gy = np.clip(x, 0, 1) * r, np.clip(y / 0.62, 0, 1) * r i, j = gx.astype(int), gy.astype(int) fx, fy = gx - i, gy - j fx, fy = fx * fx * (3 - 2 * fx), fy * fy * (3 - 2 * fy) # smoothstep top = g[j, i] * (1 - fx) + g[j, i + 1] * fx bot = g[j + 1, i] * (1 - fx) + g[j + 1, i + 1] * fx total += amp * (top * (1 - fy) + bot * fy) norm += amp; amp *= 0.5 return total / norm return sample noise = value_noise(seed=3) noise_angle = lambda x, y: noise(x, y) * 4 * np.pi ``` ::: ::: {#cell-fig-noise .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} draw(flow(noise_angle, n=2500, steps=160), GREENS, alpha=0.55) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The same particles, driven by layered value noise instead of sine waves.](index_files/figure-html/fig-noise-output-1.png){#fig-noise width=869 height=547} ::: ::: ## 5. Variations Small changes go a long way. Three to try: * **Where particles start.** Seeding them on a circle gives you rings and ribbons. * **How lines are drawn.** Thick, short and opaque reads as brush strokes, while thin, long and translucent reads as silk. * **The palette.** Dark ground with bright lines, or the reverse. ::: {#cell-fig-variations .cell fig-width='12' execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 3.4), facecolor="white", gridspec_kw={"wspace": 0.03}) t = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 900, endpoint=False) ring = (0.5 + 0.2 * np.cos(t), 0.31 + 0.2 * np.sin(t)) draw(flow(noise_angle, steps=120, starts=ring), DUSK, ax=axes[0], lw=0.8) draw(flow(noise_angle, n=900, steps=18, step_size=0.006, seed=2), GREENS, ax=axes[1], lw=3.2, alpha=0.9) draw(flow(angle, n=1600, steps=160, seed=4), [FOREST, "#197050", "#2f9b99"], bg="#eff6e9", ax=axes[2], lw=0.5, alpha=0.5) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Left: particles seeded on a circle. Middle: short, thick strokes. Right: light ground, dark lines.](index_files/figure-html/fig-variations-output-1.png){#fig-variations width=1300 height=281} ::: ::: ## 6. A finished piece Putting it together: noise field, many long paths, the blog's greens over a dark forest ground, and a scattering of lime "fireflies" where some particles end their paths. ::: {#cell-fig-final .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} paths = flow(noise_angle, n=4000, steps=180, step_size=0.003, seed=11) ax = draw(paths, GREENS[1:] + ["#2f9b99"], lw=0.45, alpha=0.5, size=(11, 6.8)) ends = paths[::25, -1] ax.scatter(ends[:, 0], ends[:, 1], s=6, color="#abff44", alpha=0.9, linewidths=0) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Forest at Dusk, 4,000 particles.](index_files/figure-html/fig-final-output-1.png){#fig-final width=950 height=597} ::: ::: ## Things to try next 1. **Stop paths from crossing.** Track which grid cells are already used and end a particle when it enters one. This gives the clean, evenly spaced look you see in a lot of plotter art. 2. **Colour by angle.** Map each segment's direction to a colour instead of picking colours by index. 3. **Animate it.** Increase `steps` frame by frame and save the frames with `matplotlib.animation`. 4. **Read the classic essay.** Tyler Hobbs' [Flow Fields](https://www.tylerxhobbs.com/words/flow-fields) is the best long read on the technique. > The field decides the shape. The particles only reveal it.
